rv.q: Mood Music is electrifyingly smart: specific yet universal, contemporary and multi-dimensional.

Or, actually, Bernard thinks he did. The fact that Cat had the lyrics papered on to her bedroom wall is by the by. Ben Chaplin is brilliant as Bernard, a man never at a loss for words, especially if they are about himself.
Roger Michell, one of the most subtle and patient of directors, makes much of the action extraordinarily telling.
It's both concise and entertaining, but at the same time you could leave after half an hour and pretty much get it.

Up to the mid-way point when Bernard upstages his protegee at an awards ceremony, the evening powers along as an immaculate, entertaining examination of collaborative processes that has the debating-chamber intensity and ambiguity of Penhall’s finest play Blue/Orange (2000).
But at the end, it felt like an album with one good track.
It’s well acted, easy to watch, rarely dull, but a bit low-calorie.
Roger Michell directs fluidly, and the central roles are expertly taken by Ben Chaplin, left, and Seana Kerslake.

Penhall cleverly choreographs the six characters as the sessions between Cat and her psychiatrist Vanessa and between Bernard and his analyst Ramsay are interspersed with the respective lawyers flinging legal arguments back and forth like shuttlecocks.

cn.t: Penhall's intelligent, zeitgeisty drama about a power struggle over songwriting credits between a manipulative male producer and young female artist earns praise for sharp writing and performances, though some find it somewhat predictable and low-calorie.
